settings.heading: The material care ceremony
settings.lede: Six steps for metal. Six for clay. Choose a material, then check the exact piece's verified instructions before cooking.
settings.metal_guide:
Read the surface

Check whether you’re looking at stainless steel, seasoned iron or carbon steel. A seasoned pan can darken with age. The model’s guide tells you what to expect.

Keep the routine with the pan

Follow the cleaning, drying and seasoning instructions for that finish. Give blades their own routine, including any care the handle needs.
settings.clay_guide:
Look for the glaze

Check the maker’s instructions for first use, cleaning and heat. Glazed and unglazed clay can call for different care.

Check what’s been tested

Chulha is a terracotta design study. Check the vessel’s record before using it to cook.

settings.title: The Polymer Covenant
settings.description: For a verified bare carbon steel surface, a very thin layer of suitable cooking oil can be heated according to its maker’s instructions to build seasoning. Stainless steel does not require this treatment. Darkening on a seasoned surface can be normal; inspect any rust or flaking.

settings.title: Thermal Discipline
settings.description: Warm the pan gradually over moderate heat before adding fat. Pre-heat time and safe heat level depend on the model and hob. Avoid heating an empty pan beyond its maker’s limits.

settings.title: Care for the Surface
settings.description: Long acidic reductions may affect a young carbon steel seasoning layer. Stainless steel has different care needs. Check the exact cooking surface before choosing wine, vinegar or citrus; there is no universal fifteen-cook embargo.

settings.title: Release the Fond
settings.description: Let the pan cool enough to handle, then loosen residue with warm water and a suitable brush or sponge. Mild soap is usually compatible with seasoned cookware when rinsed and dried; follow the finish-specific guide. Avoid long soaking where corrosion is possible.

settings.title: Leave No Water Behind
settings.description: Dry the pan and its joins thoroughly after washing. A brief low-heat dry may suit some bare metal pans, but use it only where the maker permits and never leave a pan unattended over flame.

settings.title: The Resting Membrane
settings.description: On bare carbon steel, a very thin film of food-safe oil may protect the dry surface. Buff away excess so it does not become sticky. Stainless steel needs no storage oil. Keep the piece dry with air around it.

settings.title: The Water Cure
settings.description: Check the finished vessel’s first-use instructions. Some unglazed clay cookware calls for soaking or curing; others do not. A fifteen-minute full soak is a design hypothesis here, not a universal instruction.

settings.title: Thermal Patience
settings.description: Avoid sudden temperature changes. Use a cold oven start or a gas diffuser only if the exact vessel is rated for that heat source. A 260 °C ceiling has not been verified for Chulha concepts.

settings.title: Slow Convection
settings.description: The Chulha concept is intended for gentle, moist cooking such as braising. Food-contact suitability, heat rating and acid resistance need testing for each finished glaze or unglazed surface. Do not use a concept pressure vessel for cooking.

settings.title: Return to Room Temperature
settings.description: Let a hot clay vessel cool naturally before washing. Do not plunge hot clay into cold water or set it on a cold wet surface.

settings.title: A Gentle Clean
settings.description: Use a soft sponge and warm water. Follow the maker’s instructions on detergent and whether the unglazed body can be soaked; porous surfaces can retain water and odours.

settings.title: Lid Ajar
settings.description: Let the vessel and lid dry completely before storage. Keep the lid slightly open where possible so air can circulate around the clay.
